title: Push a phase busbar up into the push-in terminals of four circuit breakers, every fork fully home
instruction: Fit the phase busbar onto the four circuit breakers, every fork fully home, and leave it there.
context: Electricians fit a phase busbar across a row of circuit breakers whenever they build or extend a distribution board, in homes as well as in industrial control panels: one comb-shaped busbar feeds every breaker instead of separate jumper wires. With push-in (quickconnect) terminals there is no screw to tighten: the busbar is pushed up into the breakers' undersides, and the fit itself makes the connection. All four forks have to be lined up under their terminals and pushed fully home together, without jamming; a fork left short is a loose connection that heats up under load.
setup: Positions are measured forward from the line joining the two arm bases (61 cm apart), left of their midline as seen from behind the robot, and up from the table top. Table: the station's light wooden table. Mounting plate: a light-grey 3 mm steel plate, 24 cm wide and 30 cm tall, stands upright on the table, fixed to it, facing the robot, its front face 33.4 cm in front of the bases, centred on the midline. DIN rail: a steel TS35 x 7.5 rail, 20 cm long, screwed across the plate, centred on the midline, its centre 17.25 cm above the table. Breakers: four white single-pole B16 miniature circuit breakers with screwless quickconnect busbar terminals (Hager MBS116, 6 kA, or equivalent), 17.5 mm wide each, about 85 mm tall, snapped side by side onto the rail and held by end stops, the row centred on the midline. Their undersides are 13 cm above the table and their front shoulders 26.8 cm in front of the bases; each breaker's busbar terminal opens in its underside, 12 mm behind the shoulder. Busbar: one single-pole insulated fork-type phase busbar for those terminals (Hager KDN163A: quickconnect, 10 mm2, 63 A, grey insulation, sold as 12 modules, or an equivalent quickconnect fork busbar), cut to four modules with an end cap on each end: about 78 mm long, 6 mm thick and 10 mm tall, with four copper forks at a 17.5 mm pitch (two tines each, about 6 mm wide and 1.2 mm thick) standing about 12 mm proud of the body, 16 g. It lies flat on its back on the table, its length running left to right and its forks pointing away from the robot, its body's centre 20 cm in front of the bases and 13 cm right of the midline.
scoring: A fork is home when the busbar's top edge, at that fork, is within 1 mm of its breaker's underside, with the fork inside that breaker's busbar terminal. The busbar is let go when both grippers are at least 5 cm from it. Tug test, once all four forks are home and both grippers have stayed at least 5 cm away for 3 s (or at the end of the run): mark the busbar's position, then pull it straight down at its middle with a spring scale, raising the pull evenly to 5 N over 1 s and holding it to 2 s. It passes if the busbar moves less than 1 mm and all four forks are still home. Score 1.0, and the run ends, once the tug has passed and the busbar stays home and let go for 1 s. Otherwise, at the end of the run: 0.2 for each fork home if the busbar is let go, and 0 if a gripper is still within 5 cm of it. Score 0 if a breaker was moved more than 2 mm along its rail or off it, or a fork was bent. Distances are read with a feeler gauge and a rule, or from a close-up photo with a scale in view.
reset_notes: Press the busbar's edge and slide it out of the terminals (the quickconnect release), then lay it back on its back in its starting place, forks away from the robot. Nothing is consumed; about 30 seconds.
fidelity: PhysX 240 Hz, station i2rt gains. Plate, rail, breakers and busbar are boxes sized from published data, not CAD. Each terminal: 10 mm slot, 1.5 mm lead-ins, fixed contact wall and a hinged, sprung push-in spring (about 0.8 N on a tine; real springs are stiffer). A 0.8 mm notch near each tine's tip (real tines are plain) stands in for the spring's one-way grip. Breakers are fixed, so 'breaker moved' is not simulated. The tug is a sim force after release. Details in README.
